title: The rule of law
subtitle: Formal and substantive conceptions, access to justice, and a live-law warning
objectives: State the difference between formal and substantive conceptions of the rule of law, and explain why the choice between them is contested rather than settled
Explain how Entick v Carrington and M v Home Office illustrate the formal, 'government under law' core of the doctrine

Evaluate R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor and the Belmarsh case as evidence for a more substantive reading, and explain why the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024 episode is now historical illustration rather than current law

leadingAuthorities.role: Foundational statement of the formal rule of law: executive action needs positive legal authority, not merely the absence of a prohibition
Access to justice as a constitutional right inherent in the rule of law, capable of invalidating a fee order that priced ordinary people out of the courts

leadingAuthorities.citation: A v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 56 (Belmarsh)
leadingAuthorities.role: Indefinite detention without trial of foreign terrorism suspects held disproportionate and discriminatory — a substantive rule-of-law and human-rights landmark

leadingAuthorities.citation: Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 (repealed by the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025)
leadingAuthorities.role: Historical case study: Parliament legislating that a court's factual finding (in R (AAA) v SSHD [2023] UKSC 42) should be treated as settled by statute — now repealed and taught as illustration, not live law

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often reach for 'no one is above the law' and stop there, treating the rule of law as a slogan rather than a doctrine with real internal disagreement. Where the profile shows knowledge outpacing application, this note appears: 'You can define it. The harder skill is arguing which conception a given fact pattern engages, and why that choice changes the answer.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well defining formal versus substantive conceptions before. The test pool below leans on application: expect scenarios where you must decide which conception is doing the work, not just recite both.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down on Part 1 and Part 2 before moving further — this lesson assumes you can state Dicey's three limbs and the formal/substantive distinction without prompting, because every later part builds an argument on top of it.

overview.hook: Every lawyer can recite it: 'no one is above the law.' Almost none of them agree on what it actually requires. Does the rule of law just mean government must act under law — any law, however unjust? Or does it mean law must meet some minimum standard of fairness before it counts at all? This is one of the oldest live arguments in public law, and unlike sovereignty, it has never been resolved by a single case or Act. This lesson gives you both sides, and then a case study — now closed, but recently very much open — of what happens when the two collide.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. IMPORTANT CURRENCY NOTE: the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024, discussed in this lesson as a rule-of-law case study, was repealed by the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 (Royal Assent 2 December 2025). Older textbooks, lecture notes and past exam commentary written before December 2025 may still discuss the Rwanda Act as though it were live legislation — it is not. Nothing in this lesson should be read as describing current immigration or asylum law. It is retained solely as a worked illustration of the underlying rule-of-law and separation-of-powers debate: whether, and how far, Parliament may legislate that a court's finding of fact is to be treated as settled. That debate outlives the repealed Act; the Act itself does not.

parts.heading: Two people, both right, arguing about the same three words
parts.voice: philosophical — sets up a genuine dispute as a dispute, refusing to resolve it before the student has felt its force
body: Imagine two constitutional lawyers. The first says: 'the rule of law simply means government must act through law — clear, general, publicly known, prospective rules, applied equally, with access to a court to test compliance. What the law actually says is a separate question, for democracy to answer, not for lawyers to police.' Call this the formal conception.

The second says: 'that can't be right. A state that passes a clear, general, publicly known, prospectively-applied law authorising torture, or removing a whole group's access to any court whatsoever, has not honoured the rule of law just because it followed the right procedure. Some substantive minimum — fair process, basic rights, genuine access to justice — has to be built into the concept itself, or the phrase does no real work.' Call this the substantive conception.

Both lawyers can quote real authority. Both are taken seriously by serious courts. This lesson does not resolve the disagreement, because English public law has not resolved it — Lord Bingham, perhaps the most influential modern judicial voice on the rule of law, wrote an entire book defending a substantive reading, while critics have argued that the concept becomes unworkably vague the moment it absorbs 'good law' rather than merely 'law, applied as law.' What you need is not a verdict, but fluency in both positions and the confidence to say, in an exam, which one a given case or fact pattern is really testing.

components.definition: The rule of law as a set of procedural and structural qualities a legal system must have — clarity, generality, prospectivity, equal application, judicial accessibility — without regard to whether the content of the law is itself just.

The rule of law as also requiring some minimum content — protection of fundamental rights, fair process, genuine access to justice — such that a law can fail the rule of law even if it was validly and clearly enacted.

interaction.prompt: A state passes a clear, publicly known, prospective law authorising indefinite arbitrary detention of a disfavoured minority, applied consistently to everyone in that group. On the FORMAL conception alone, does this comply with the rule of law?
options: Yes — the formal conception asks only about the law's procedural qualities, not its content
No — the formal conception also requires the content of the law to be substantively just
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct, and notice how uncomfortable that answer feels — that discomfort is exactly the intuition the substantive conception is trying to capture. Keep both readings in mind as we go through the authorities.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: On the formal conception specifically, the answer is yes, however troubling that sounds — it asks only about form (clarity, generality, prospectivity, equal application), not content. That gap between the formal answer and your instinct is precisely why the substantive conception exists as a rival.

parts.heading: 1765: the formal core, stated before the phrase existed
parts.voice: historical close-reading — treats an 18th-century judgment as a text to be read carefully, not summarised
body: Entick v Carrington predates Dicey's famous formulation of the rule of law by over a century, but it states the formal core more sharply than most modern textbooks manage. King's messengers, acting under a warrant issued by the Secretary of State, broke into John Entick's house, searched it, and seized his papers, on suspicion of seditious libel. There was no statute and no established common law power specifically authorising such a search warrant.

The Secretary of State's defence amounted to: nothing expressly forbade it, and general warrants of this kind were a long-standing government practice. Lord Camden CJ rejected this outright. His reasoning is the sentence every public lawyer eventually memorises: if it is law, show me the book that says so — and if no book, no statute, no precedent authorises the power claimed, then the officers who exercised it are as liable as any private trespasser, regardless of their office.

The structural point matters as much as the outcome. Entick establishes that the executive's powers must be positively found in law — a grant, not merely an absence of prohibition — while private individuals may do anything the law does not forbid. That asymmetry, official power needs a source, private freedom does not, is the formal rule of law's oldest and most durable content, and it survives untouched by every substantive-conception debate that came after it.

components.factsShort: King's messengers, acting on a Secretary of State's warrant with no clear legal basis, broke into John Entick's house and seized his papers on suspicion of seditious libel.
components.ratioShort: Executive officials require positive legal authority for their actions; the absence of a prohibition is not enough, and officials without such authority are liable in trespass like anyone else.

expanded.facts: Entick's home was entered and searched pursuant to a general warrant issued by the Secretary of State, on suspicion that Entick had authored seditious material. No statute or established common law doctrine authorised warrants of this kind for this purpose; the practice had simply grown up as a matter of executive convenience.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Camden CJ held that the power to enter and search a person's house and seize their papers could not be justified by mere government practice or the absence of an express prohibition. 'If it is law, it will be found in our books. If it is not to be found there, it is not law.' Because no source of law authorised the warrant, the messengers who executed it were trespassers, and the Secretary of State's office gave them no immunity.
expanded.significance: Entick is the founding statement of the principle later developed as 'no one, however high, is above the law' — but its precise, formal content is narrower and sharper than that slogan: official action requires a positive legal source of authority, and cannot simply rely on the absence of a prohibition the way private conduct can. It says nothing, on its own, about whether the content of a properly-authorised law must also be substantively fair — that is the gap the rest of this lesson explores.

interaction.prompt: In this short passage adapted from Lord Camden CJ's reasoning in Entick v Carrington, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
interaction.passage: The messengers argued that similar warrants had long been issued as a matter of practice, and that no statute expressly forbade this one. But if the power exercised here is a lawful power, it must be shown to rest on some positive authority — statute, or established principle of common law. If no such authority can be found, the power does not exist, whatever the practice has been, and those who exercised it are liable in trespass exactly as a private person would be.
interaction.ratioSentence: If no such authority can be found, the power does not exist, whatever the practice has been, and those who exercised it are liable in trespass exactly as a private person would be.

parts.heading: Pricing people out of court: UNISON and the substantive turn
parts.voice: argumentative — builds a case for the substantive conception using a modern example, then invites scrutiny of it
body: Fast-forward to 2017. The Lord Chancellor had introduced fees for bringing a claim in an employment tribunal — up to £1,200 for some claims — using a general statutory power to set court fees. Nothing about the fee order was procedurally improper: it was made under a clear statutory power, applied consistently, and published in advance. On the formal conception alone, there is little to object to.

UNISON challenged it anyway, and won, on rule-of-law grounds. The Supreme Court held that the right of access to justice is inherent in the rule of law itself, and is protected not merely as a matter of ordinary administrative law but as a constitutional common law right — one that general statutory words will not be read as overriding unless Parliament makes its intention to do so unmistakably clear. The fees, set at a level that made bringing many genuine claims economically irrational, were held unlawful because they effectively closed off access to justice for a real class of claimants, whatever the formal validity of the power under which they were made.

This is the clearest modern illustration of the substantive conception actually deciding a case, not just featuring in academic commentary. The formal lawyer from Part 1 has a response, though, and you should be able to give it: perhaps UNISON isn't really a substantive-conception case at all, but a formal one in disguise — access to a court to enforce your legal rights is itself part of the formal apparatus (a court that is genuinely open, not merely open on paper), so the case can be read as formal rule-of-law reasoning applied rigorously, without conceding anything to a substantive theory of justice. Which reading you prefer is, again, a genuinely open question.

components.label: UNISON: the reasoning in three steps
points: Access to justice is not a mere policy preference; it is inherent in the rule of law and protected as a constitutional common law right

General words in a statutory fee-setting power will not be read as authorising fees that make access to justice practically unavailable to a real class of claimants, absent express and specific statutory language
The fee order was therefore ultra vires — outside the power actually granted — and unlawful, without Parliament needing to have said so expressly

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that most directly engages the UNISON access-to-justice reasoning.
interaction.scenarioText: A government minister, acting under a broad and clearly worded statutory power to 'regulate the conduct of proceedings' in a specialist tribunal, introduces a new rule requiring claimants to pay a non-refundable administrative fee of £3,000 before a claim can be lodged — a sum that exceeds the value of most claims the tribunal typically hears and that most claimants cannot afford.
tappableSpans: broad and clearly worded statutory power
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The formal validity of the power is not in dispute here — the fee-setting power is clear and general, exactly like the power in UNISON. What triggers the access-to-justice reasoning is the practical effect: a fee level that genuinely prices ordinary claimants out of bringing claims at all.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The formal source of power (a clearly worded statutory power) is not the issue — that part is uncontroversial, just as it was in UNISON. Look instead for the fact showing the practical effect on ordinary claimants' ability to actually use the tribunal.

parts.heading: Belmarsh: rights, discrimination, and a doctrine stretched to its limit
parts.voice: case-narrative — slows down on the facts because the stakes, not just the doctrine, are the point
body: After the September 2001 attacks, Parliament enacted powers under the Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001 allowing the indefinite detention, without trial or charge, of foreign nationals suspected of involvement in terrorism who could not be deported (often because deportation would expose them to torture or death abroad). The power applied only to foreign nationals — British citizens suspected of the same conduct could not be detained this way at all.

The House of Lords, sitting as a nine-member panel because of the case's constitutional weight, held the detention powers incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights. Two strands of reasoning stand out. First, proportionality: indefinite detention without trial was a more drastic interference with liberty than the threat genuinely required, particularly given other, less intrusive measures were available. Second, and more distinctively, discrimination: since the power targeted only foreign nationals, when the underlying threat (terrorism) was not in fact confined to foreign nationals, the scheme was irrational as well as discriminatory — it responded to a supposedly national emergency with a measure that left an equivalent domestic threat completely unaddressed.

Belmarsh matters here because it shows the substantive conception doing real constitutional work at the highest level, against a democratically enacted statute, in the middle of a genuine security crisis — exactly the circumstances in which a purely formal conception would offer the least resistance. It is also, not coincidentally, the case courts and commentators reach for whenever a later government tries something structurally similar: a factual claim of emergency used to justify detaining or restricting a defined class of people more harshly than anyone else. Keep it in mind for Part 5.

components.text: If the court is satisfied that the provision is incompatible with a Convention right, it may make a declaration of that incompatibility.
elements: A declaration of incompatibility does not itself strike down or invalidate the offending provision
It leaves the provision in force unless and until Parliament chooses to amend it
It is the remedy the House of Lords used in Belmarsh, prompting Parliament to replace the detention powers with control orders

interaction.prompt: A fictional Act permits indefinite detention without trial of any non-citizen suspected of involvement in organised cybercrime, on the basis that citizens cannot be deported and so pose a lesser ongoing risk once released on bail conditions, while non-citizens facing deportation risk absconding. A detained claimant argues the scheme is discriminatory and disproportionate, relying on Belmarsh. Analyse the claim.
factsToOrder: The power applies only to non-citizens, not citizens suspected of the same conduct
The stated justification distinguishes non-citizens on a specific, articulated risk (absconding pending deportation), not merely nationality as such
The measure is indefinite detention without trial, the most intrusive measure available
The claimant is a non-citizen detained under the power

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the fictional detention scheme is disproportionate and unjustifiably discriminatory, applying the reasoning in Belmarsh.
modelAnswer.rule: Indefinite detention without trial is a highly intrusive measure that must be shown to be a proportionate response to the threat addressed; a scheme that distinguishes between groups (e.g. citizens and non-citizens) exposed to the same underlying risk, without a rationally connected justification for that distinction, is liable to be found discriminatory and therefore disproportionate, following Belmarsh.
modelAnswer.application: Unlike the scheme in Belmarsh, this fictional Act offers an articulated reason for distinguishing non-citizens — absconding risk pending deportation — rather than nationality as a bare proxy for dangerousness. That is a stronger justification than Belmarsh's scheme had. But the measure remains indefinite detention without trial, the most intrusive option available, and the claimant can still argue less drastic alternatives (such as bail with reporting and residence conditions, as eventually used for citizens and non-citizens alike after Belmarsh) would address the absconding risk without indefinite detention.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The scheme is more defensible than the one struck down in Belmarsh because its distinction is tied to a specific, articulated risk rather than nationality alone, but it remains vulnerable to a proportionality challenge unless the government can show indefinite detention, rather than a less intrusive alternative, is genuinely necessary to address that specific risk.

parts.heading: When Parliament tells a court its facts were wrong: the Rwanda episode
parts.voice: case-study-with-warning — deliberately marks itself as closed history throughout, refusing to let the reader forget it
body: A note before this part begins, not after it: everything described here is history. The Act discussed was repealed in December 2025. It is included because it is, even now, the sharpest teaching example of a genuine rule-of-law collision — not because any of it is current law.

In November 2023, in R (AAA) v Secretary of State for the Home Department, the Supreme Court unanimously held that removing asylum seekers to Rwanda under the Government's policy was unlawful, because there were substantial grounds for believing asylum seekers sent there faced a real risk of refoulement — being returned onward to their country of origin, where they might face persecution, contrary to the UK's obligations. That is a finding of fact about conditions in Rwanda and about the Rwandan asylum system, reached after evidence was examined by three levels of court.

The Government's response was the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024. Its central and most constitutionally striking feature was a statutory declaration that Rwanda is to be treated as a safe country, disapplying parts of the Human Rights Act 1998 and substantially limiting the ability of courts to consider evidence about actual safety in individual cases. In effect, Parliament legislated that a factual question the Supreme Court had just answered one way should thereafter be treated by courts as answered the other way.

This is where the formal and substantive conceptions genuinely pull apart, rather than just disagreeing in theory. On a strictly formal view, there is nothing objectionable in principle: Parliament is sovereign, a statute is a statute, clearly worded and prospectively applied, and courts must apply it — Parliament overriding a judicial finding by ordinary legislation is exactly what parliamentary sovereignty permits, however unusual. On a substantive view, something has gone wrong regardless of the formal validity: a court's considered factual finding, reached on evidence, was legislated away rather than tested by better evidence, and access to a court capable of genuinely reviewing the safety question on the merits was curtailed — echoing UNISON's insistence that access to justice must be real, not merely available on paper. The Act's repeal in December 2025 (following a change of policy, not a court ruling striking it down) means this argument was never resolved by a court either; it simply became moot when the Act it was about ceased to exist. That is exactly why it remains useful to you: as a clean illustration of the two conceptions in genuine tension, with the historical outcome (repeal) telling you nothing about which conception is 'right'.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students sometimes write about the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024 as though it were current immigration law, applying it to a present-day fact pattern or citing it as the operative legal test for removals.
components.whyItsWrong: The Act was repealed by the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 (Royal Assent 2 December 2025). It has no current legal effect and should never be applied to a live fact pattern in an exam answer. Its only proper use is as a historical rule-of-law case study — citing it correctly means saying explicitly that it is repealed and explaining what the episode illustrates about the tension between formal and substantive conceptions, not treating it as good law.

interaction.prompt: As at September 2026, what is the correct legal status of the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024?
options: It remains in force and governs current asylum removals to Rwanda
It has been repealed by the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 and has no current legal effect
It was struck down by the courts as incompatible with the rule of law
interaction.trapExplanation: The first option is the mistake older materials can lead students into — the Act is not current law. The third is also wrong, and for an important reason: the Act was not struck down or invalidated by any court (courts cannot invalidate a UK Act of Parliament); it was repealed by a later Act, an ordinary exercise of parliamentary sovereignty, following a change of government policy. Distinguishing 'repealed by Parliament' from 'struck down by a court' matters — it is itself an illustration of the formal conception's point that only Parliament, not the courts, can undo an Act of Parliament.

testPool.prompt: Name the two competing conceptions of the rule of law this lesson contrasts.
acceptableAnswers: the formal conception and the substantive conception
testPool.modelAnswer: The formal conception, which asks only whether law has the right procedural qualities (clarity, generality, prospectivity, equal application, access to a court), and the substantive conception, which also requires some minimum content, such as protection of fundamental rights and genuine access to justice.

testPool.prompt: In Entick v Carrington, did the absence of an express legal prohibition on the search justify the King's messengers' conduct?
options: No — executive officials need positive legal authority for their actions; absence of prohibition is not enough
Yes — officials, like private individuals, may do anything not expressly forbidden

testPool.prompt: What did R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor decide?
options: That employment tribunal fees set at a level that made bringing many genuine claims economically irrational were unlawful, because access to justice is inherent in the rule of law
That employment tribunals could no longer charge any fees under any circumstances, as a matter of statute
That the Lord Chancellor had no statutory power to set court or tribunal fees at all
testPool.trapExplanation: The Lord Chancellor did have a general statutory power to set fees — the case did not deny that power exists, and did not create a blanket ban on any fees whatsoever. The issue was that this particular fee level, in practice, priced ordinary claimants out of using the tribunal at all, which the general statutory words did not clearly authorise.

testPool.prompt: In the Belmarsh case, did the detention powers under challenge apply equally to British citizens and foreign nationals suspected of the same terrorism-related conduct?
options: No — they applied only to foreign nationals who could not be deported
Yes — the powers applied to any suspect regardless of nationality

testPool.prompt: What does a declaration of incompatibility under s 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, the remedy used in Belmarsh, actually do to the offending provision?
options: It leaves the provision formally in force; it does not strike it down, but signals incompatibility and leaves the response to Parliament
It automatically repeals the incompatible provision with immediate effect
It suspends the provision until the European Court of Human Rights rules on it

testPool.prompt: In the extract below, adapted from the reasoning in R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor, highlight the sentence stating the ratio.
testPool.passage: The Lord Chancellor had a broad power to prescribe fees for proceedings, and the fee order was made using clear statutory language. But the right of access to the courts is not merely a matter of policy; it is inherent in the rule of law, and general words in a statute will not be read as permitting fees that make it, in practice, futile for a substantial number of people to bring proceedings at all.
testPool.ratioSentence: But the right of access to the courts is not merely a matter of policy; it is inherent in the rule of law, and general words in a statute will not be read as permitting fees that make it, in practice, futile for a substantial number of people to bring proceedings at all.

testPool.prompt: A local authority, under a general statutory power to 'manage the use of public parks', introduces a rule banning all political leafleting in every park, at all times, without exception. A campaigner argues this breaches the rule of law on substantive grounds. Which best captures the substantive-conception argument available here?
options: A blanket, exceptionless ban on political expression in all public spaces the authority controls goes beyond what a general management power should be read as authorising, echoing UNISON's insistence that general words will not be read as authorising a serious practical curtailment of a fundamental activity
The rule of law has nothing to say here because the ban is clearly worded, general, prospective and applied equally to everyone
The rule is automatically invalid because it was made by a local authority rather than by Parliament
testPool.explanation: The second option describes the formal conception's answer, not the substantive one the question asks for — under a purely formal analysis this rule might indeed pass. The substantive argument, by analogy with UNISON, is that a general power should not lightly be read as authorising a serious, blanket curtailment of a fundamental activity (here, political expression) without much clearer statutory words. The third option is simply wrong as a matter of administrative law: local authorities can validly exercise delegated statutory powers.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that makes this scenario most closely resemble the Belmarsh reasoning, rather than a straightforward, unobjectionable security measure.
testPool.scenarioText: In response to a rise in a particular category of serious fraud, the Government introduces enhanced reporting obligations for a class of regulated financial firms, requiring them to notify a supervisor of suspicious transactions within 24 hours, breach of which carries a substantial fine.
tappableSpans: rise in a particular category of serious fraud
notify a supervisor of suspicious transactions within 24 hours
testPool.explanation: None of the tappable facts here actually resembles Belmarsh, which is the point of this item: this scenario is a proportionate, non-discriminatory, non-detentive regulatory response, not an indefinite-detention or liberty-restricting measure targeted at one group. 'Enhanced reporting obligations' is the closest thing to a 'measure' in the passage, but tapping it (or any other span) should prompt you to notice there is no detention, no group-based distinction and no comparably drastic interference with liberty at all — the scenario is deliberately built to NOT be a Belmarsh case, testing whether you can recognise the absence of the trigger facts rather than assume every security-related scenario is one.

testPool.prompt: Which of these two scenarios more closely engages the Entick v Carrington principle, rather than the UNISON principle?
testPool.scenarioA: A police officer, with no statutory power or common law authority to do so, enters and searches a private home without a warrant, relying only on the absence of any law expressly forbidding it.
testPool.scenarioB: A government department, under a valid and clearly worded statutory power, sets an application fee for a public benefit scheme so high that most eligible claimants cannot afford to apply.
testPool.explanation: Scenario A is Entick: executive action with no positive source of legal authority at all, defended only by the absence of a prohibition — the formal rule-of-law point that official power must be affirmatively granted. Scenario B is UNISON: a validly and clearly granted power, exercised in a way that, in substance, defeats a fundamental right (here, access to a benefit scheme rather than a court, but the same structural argument) — the source of power is not in question, only whether its exercise should be read as authorised given the practical effect.

testPool.prompt: A public body relies on a broadly worded statutory power to 'take such steps as are necessary to secure public order' to close, indefinitely and without any route of appeal, all public spaces to a named category of protest group, while allowing other groups to continue protesting on the same topics. A challenge is brought relying on both Entick and UNISON-style reasoning. Analyse the challenge.
factsToOrder: The power relied on is broadly worded, not specific to protest closures
The closure applies indefinitely, with no route of appeal
The closure targets one named category of protest group while allowing others on the same topics to continue
No individualised justification is given for why this group, specifically, threatens public order more than others

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the closure power was lawfully exercised, applying both the Entick requirement of positive legal authority and the UNISON/substantive-conception concern about practical denial of a fundamental activity.
modelAnswer.rule: Under Entick, executive action requires a genuine source of legal authority for what is actually done, not merely a broadly worded power that could be stretched to cover it; under UNISON, general statutory words will not readily be read as authorising a measure that, in substance, denies a fundamental right or activity to a defined group without clear and specific justification.
modelAnswer.application: The power is general ('take such steps as necessary to secure public order') and was not drafted with indefinite, appealless, group-targeted closures in mind — an Entick-style argument that the specific measure taken exceeds what the general grant can fairly be read to authorise. Layered onto this is the UNISON-style substantive concern: an indefinite ban with no appeal route, applied to one group while others continue, functions as a practical denial of the right to protest for that group specifically, without any individualised justification distinguishing their risk from anyone else's — echoing the discrimination strand of Belmarsh as much as UNISON's access-to-justice reasoning.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The closure is vulnerable to challenge on both grounds: it likely exceeds the genuine scope of the statutory power (Entick), and, even if within its literal words, it is the kind of exercise of that power the courts will scrutinise closely and likely refuse to treat as authorised, given its indefinite, appealless, group-targeted effect (UNISON/Belmarsh-style substantive reasoning).

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 remains part of current UK law today?
sliderLabels: Repealed and no longer in force
testPool.explanation: The Act was repealed by the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 (Royal Assent 2 December 2025). It has no current legal effect and should be treated in any exam answer purely as a historical rule-of-law case study, never as governing law for a present-day fact pattern.

testPool.prompt: What did the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 do that made it such a sharp rule-of-law case study, before its repeal?
options: It statutorily declared Rwanda safe and limited courts' ability to consider evidence otherwise, in effect legislatively overriding a factual finding the Supreme Court had just reached in R (AAA) v SSHD
It was the first Act of Parliament ever held unlawful by a UK court
It removed the Home Secretary's power to make any immigration decisions at all
testPool.trapExplanation: No UK court can hold an Act of Parliament unlawful or strike it down — that is inconsistent with parliamentary sovereignty and was never the constitutional mechanism at issue here, before or after repeal. The third option misdescribes the Act's content entirely. The genuine rule-of-law tension was Parliament legislating a factual conclusion (Rwanda's safety) that a court had just found otherwise on the evidence, and narrowing the scope for courts to reconsider that finding case by case.

testPool.prompt: Was the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 repealed by a court ruling, or by a later Act of Parliament?
options: By a later Act of Parliament — the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025
By a court ruling that it was incompatible with the rule of law

testPool.prompt: Put these events in the Rwanda policy litigation and legislative history in order.
items: Government develops a policy to remove certain asylum seekers to Rwanda
Supreme Court holds in R (AAA) v SSHD that removals are unlawful given a real risk of refoulement
Parliament enacts the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024, declaring Rwanda safe by statute
Parliament repeals the Act via the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025

testPool.prompt: A student's exam answer, written in 2026, states: 'Under the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024, Rwanda is conclusively deemed a safe country for the purposes of any asylum removal decision.' Assessed against the currency point this lesson raises, what is the central problem with this answer?
options: It states repealed legislation as though it were current law, without acknowledging the 2025 repeal — a serious currency error regardless of how accurately it describes what the 2024 Act once said
There is no problem; the description of the Act's original effect is accurate
The problem is that the description of the Act's original effect is inaccurate, not that it is out of date
testPool.explanation: The description of what the 2024 Act originally did may well be accurate — that is not where the error lies. The problem is currency: presenting a repealed Act as current, operative law is a serious error in any public law answer, and examiners will penalise it even where the underlying description of the (former) legal position is otherwise correct. Always flag repeal explicitly when using the Rwanda Act as an example.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The two most common mistakes in this lesson: collapsing the formal and substantive conceptions into one idea instead of arguing which one a fact pattern engages, and treating the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024 as live law rather than the repealed historical case study it now is. Both mistakes come from the same habit — reaching for a label instead of checking what is actually being asked and whether the source is still current.
